name: Air-cooled vs liquid-cooled is a per-SKU form-factor fact, not an architecture fact: H100 PCIe is dual-slot air-cooled, H100 SXM is a bare module
notes: THIS RECORD EXISTS TO KILL A COMMON ERROR IN POWER-DENSITY PLANNING: THE MENTAL MODEL THAT 'HOPPER IS AIR-COOLED AND BLACKWELL IS LIQUID-COOLED' IS WRONG AT THE PART LEVEL. NVIDIA's H100 datasheet form-factor row reads, verbatim and side by side: 'SXM' for H100 SXM and 'PCIe dual-slot air-cooled' for H100 PCIe. The word 'air-cooled' is attached to a specific SKU's physical form factor, in the same row as its Max TDP of 350 W, not to the Hopper architecture as a whole. So: H100 PCIe at 350 W IS air-cooled and goes in a conventional server in a conventional colo with no liquid anywhere. H100 SXM at 700 W is a bare module with no cooler, normally deployed in an HGX baseboard or DGX system, which is itself air-cooled at the node level - see supply/dgx-h100-h200-10kw-air-cooled-node, which documents a 10.2 kW max air-cooled 8-GPU node with 1105 CFM of front-to-back airflow. The H100 NVL sits between the two, typically shipped as a PCIe card with a factory cooler. THE CONSEQUENCE FOR ANY POWER-DENSITY DECISION: you cannot ask 'is this chip air-cooled or liquid-cooled'. You have to ask what the specific SKU's form factor and TDP are, then what the host chassis is, then what the facility is. A 350 W air-cooled H100 PCIe and a 700 W SXM H100 are both 'Hopper', differ by 2x in power, and can have completely different facility requirements. ALSO WORTH FLAGGING FOR POWER SIZING: NVIDIA's HGX H100/H200 datasheet publishes NO TDP and NO rack power figure at all - only the Hopper SXM datasheet gives 700 W - so anyone power-sizing an HGX baseboard must derive it from the SXM datasheet and mark it as derived rather than vendor-stated. That asymmetry between generations is itself a signal: every Blackwell platform datasheet publishes Max TDP per GPU, while the Hopper HGX datasheet publishes none, because Blackwell customers had to spec for facility integration from the start.
